items.title: Fair Cost of Care rates for direct payments (self-directed support Option 1)

items.plain: Angus is considering paying set Fair Cost of Care rates when people arrange their own care with a direct payment. It wants views from care at home providers, personal assistants, their employers who get direct payments, and staff.
items.detail: The Engage Angus page for care at home providers says the council is considering the Fair Cost of Care rates for Option 1 (direct payments), which are already used in Options 2 and 3 in Angus, and that feedback will help it understand the impact of set rates and inform any future decisions. Engage Angus lists separate surveys for personal assistants, staff, care at home providers and direct payment recipients; I could open only the care at home providers page. The surveys are anonymous. The partnership's social media post says the personal assistant survey closes on 23 October 2026 and will help inform future discussions about PA rates; I could not open the post itself, and I did not confirm whether the other surveys close on the same day. What the rates are, and whether they would change direct payment amounts, is not stated on the page I read. On 26 October 2026 the Engage Angus pages for personal assistants, staff, care at home providers and direct payment recipients were all still listed as published with survey links, but none showed a closing date; it is listed as Watch, not Open, for that reason.
items.how: Choose the survey for your role on Engage Angus (search the projects list for 'Rates'). If you are unsure which applies to you, ask the Angus Health and Social Care Partnership.

items.title: Council reform: proposal for regional and community authorities
items.body: Scottish Government (Local Government and Housing Directorate)
items.time: discussion paper published 21 September 2026; no public response form or closing date found on 14 October 2026; the government wants a shared direction before the end of 2026
items.plain: An opening proposal to replace Scotland's 32 councils with 6 to 10 regional authorities and 120 to 160 community authorities. Local news reports say Dundee, Angus and Perth and Kinross could be merged into one Tayside authority.
items.detail: The paper says regional authorities would handle strategic matters such as economic development, housing, strategic planning, transport, waste and education, and community authorities would handle local decisions such as householder planning applications, licensing, green spaces, town centre regeneration and local leisure and culture. Councillors would still be elected by ward and sit on both. Social care and social work are part of the same three-month dialogue. The paper does not name the regions; the possible Tayside merger comes from reports in The Courier, not from the paper. The dialogue is mainly with councils, COSLA, trade unions and care providers; the paper says more detailed proposals will follow for Parliament, councils and communities. I found no form for members of the public to respond.
items.how: No public consultation is open. Read the paper, and contact your councillors or MSP if you want to give a view. Watch for the more detailed proposals the government says will follow.

items.title: Legal aid reform

items.detail: The hub showed it as closing on 13 October 2026, and it was no longer on the hub's open list on 14 October 2026. It consulted on a new Legal Aid (Scotland) Bill: a clear purpose and objectives for legal aid set by Scottish Ministers, fewer and simpler aid types, simpler eligibility, contributions and repayments, data sharing with bodies such as Social Security Scotland to ease benefit passporting, a voluntary 'high-trust' model for accredited solicitors, and the option to commission services through grants, contracts or directly employed solicitors. The page says legal aid should stay broadly available and targeted at those least able to pay. There are 22 questions, an Easy Read version and British Sign Language translations.

items.title: Ending student tenancies in purpose-built student accommodation
items.time: closed 22 October 2026; no outcome found on 26 October 2026
items.plain: Closed. When students living in purpose-built student accommodation should be allowed to end their tenancy early, what evidence they would need, and how the process should work. It applies across Scotland, including student halls and private student blocks in Dundee.
items.detail: The Housing (Scotland) Act 2025 lets Scottish Ministers make regulations so students in purpose-built student accommodation can end a tenancy in set circumstances. At present these tenancies run for a fixed term matching the academic year and students must pay for the whole period, even if they leave. The consultation proposes a list of circumstances, a 28-day notice period with up to 20 more days to ask for further evidence, and asks what a fair way to challenge a refusal would be. There are four questions. The page asks for views from students who have lived in this kind of accommodation, their families, universities and colleges, student representative councils, and providers, developers and investors. The page does not name Dundee; the link to Dundee's students is my reading.
items.how: The consultation has closed; it was no longer on the hub's open list on 26 October 2026. Watch the hub for the published responses.

items.title: Dundee visitor levy: have your say
items.time: closing time not stated on the page
items.plain: A small charge on overnight stays in Dundee. Two options: 5% of the nightly room rate, or a flat £5 per room per night, both capped at seven nights.
items.detail: Opened 31 August 2026 under the Visitor Levy (Scotland) Act 2024. Applies to hotels, guesthouses, B&Bs, hostels, self-catering and short-term lets. Money must be held separately, reported each year and spent only on visitor facilities and services. Dundee had over 1.4 million visitors in 2024, with more than 600,000 overnight stays. Councillors decide after the consultation. If approved, Scottish law needs at least 18 months' notice, so the earliest start is 2028/29. Paper copies are at The McManus and the Central Library; events are listed on Eventbrite, and a council social media post lists a session at the Central Library on Tuesday 20 October, 10.30am to 12.30pm. An Eventbrite listing also shows an online session on Wednesday 21 October (10am to 11.30am UK time, converted from the time zone the listing showed me). Business sessions run through Dundee and Angus Chamber of Commerce.
items.how: Take the roughly 10-minute online survey, use a paper copy, or phone 01382 549946.

items.title: Montrose Golf Links: proposed 99-year lease
items.time: closed 9 October 2026; results go to a full council meeting, date not found on 12 October 2026
items.plain: Angus Council proposes leasing Montrose Golf Links, a Common Good asset, for 99 years to Montrose Golf Links Ltd, with The Ancient Links Golf Company running the courses. It closed on 9 October. It is in Montrose, but it is a guide to how Angus may handle golf links such as Carnoustie's.
items.detail: Statutory consultation under section 104 of the Community Empowerment (Scotland) Act 2015, which opened on 13 August 2026. Proposals: at least £3 million of investment in the first five years, rent of £30,000 a year to the Montrose Common Good Fund, public access to the 1562 and Broomfield courses, and priority and discounted prices for Angus residents. Results go to a full council meeting, and the lease would also need Sheriff Court approval.

items.detail: Inch Cape is being built about 15 to 22km off the Angus coast and is expected to be fully operational in 2027, run from a new base at the Port of Montrose. It is in Montrose, so it is shown under Carnoustie as an Angus comparison; charities and community councils are invited to respond.

items.title: Community pharmacy services in Tayside: public survey
items.time: survey posted by NHS Tayside on 5 October 2026; the post gives no closing date or time, so check the survey before you rely on it
items.plain: NHS Tayside wants to hear from people across Tayside, including Dundee, Broughty Ferry, Monifieth and Carnoustie, about using their local community pharmacy and what they know about the services it offers.
items.detail: NHS Tayside's social media post says community pharmacies dispense prescriptions, give advice and treatment for minor illnesses, and support people with their medicines and other health needs. The survey asks about your experience of using community pharmacy services and your awareness of what is available. NHS Tayside says the feedback will help it understand local needs, find where improvements may be needed and raise awareness of the services. The survey takes about 10 minutes. The link in the post is a shortened tinyurl address, and I could not open the survey itself, so I could not see a closing date. It is listed as Watch, not Open, for that reason.
items.how: Follow the survey link in NHS Tayside's post (the button below opens the same short link).

people: People across Tayside who use community pharmacies
Older people and people taking several medicines
systems: Community pharmacy services and health advice

items.title: Bield rent plans 2027/28: stage one tenant survey (charity)
items.body: Bield Housing and Care (charity and housing association)
items.time: stage one survey closed 16 October 2026; Bield says a wider consultation with rent options will follow later in the year, date not announced
items.plain: Bield, a housing charity for older people with homes in Angus and across Scotland, asked its tenants what matters most before it sets rent options for 2027/28. A second consultation with costed rent options is due later in the year.
items.detail: Bield's page says this was the first stage of its rent consultation, to understand tenants' priorities before it develops detailed rent proposals; decisions affect what tenants pay and the services, investment and support Bield can provide. The later consultation will set out proposed rent options and what each means for tenants in pounds and pence. The survey was for Bield tenants only. Bield's site lists homes such as Clyde Court in Arbroath and Ashgrove Court in Blairgowrie; I did not check which Bield homes are in Dundee, Broughty Ferry, Monifieth or Carnoustie.
items.how: Stage one has closed. Bield tenants should watch for the second-stage consultation on Bield's website or contact Bield.

people: Bield tenants, mainly older people, including in Angus

items.title: Scottish Planning Biodiversity Metric
items.time: closing time not stated on the page
items.plain: A proposed standard way to measure how big developments affect wildlife habitats, and whether they leave nature better off, used in planning decisions across Scotland, including Dundee and Angus.
items.detail: Opened 31 August 2026 for 13 weeks. The metric adapts England's biodiversity metric to Scotland and supports National Planning Framework 4 policy 3b, which says national, major or EIA developments should only be supported if they deliver significant biodiversity enhancements. It includes a user guide, an Excel calculation tool and habitat condition sheets (which may not suit assistive technology). NatureScot also wants feedback on a rapid assessment tool for peatland. Version 1 is expected in spring 2027. There are no plans for Scottish legislation on biodiversity metrics.
items.how: Respond on NatureScot's Commonplace consultation site. You can also use the Word form and email it, or write to NatureScot, Meadowbank House, 153 London Road, Edinburgh EH8 7AU.
